records.table: Glenmorangie The Original is the Highland single malt from Tain, made in stills with necks over five metres tall and aged twelve years in bourbon casks. Expect citrus, peach and vanilla, then almond and coconut; pour it neat with a little water.
records.story: By the house's own account, a farmer and his wife set about building a distillery at Tain in 1843, turning the old Morangie brewery on their land into a still house. With no money for new stills, they bought a pair of second-hand stills that had made gin. The stills that followed are tall ones too: their copper necks stand 5.14 metres, the height, the house likes to say, of a giraffe. For decades a staff of sixteen ran the distillery, remembered as the Sixteen Men of Tain. In 1918 the distillery was sold to Macdonald & Muir, a firm that renamed itself after its malt in 1996, and in 2004 the company was sold to Louis Vuitton Moët Hennessy. For years the flagship was a ten-year-old called The Original. In July 2024 the house gave it twelve years in bourbon casks, keeping the name and the strength, after its tasting panel found that the two extra years added sweetness and a silkier body. Behind a bar it is the plain lesson in what tall stills and American oak alone give a malt: fruit, flowers and vanilla, with no sherry in it.

records.table: Oban 14 Year Old is the single malt from the small distillery in the middle of the West Highland port of Oban, made in two small stills cooled by worm tubs. Expect orange zest, fruit bread and clove with a dry, minty finish; pour it neat with water.
records.story: Two brothers set up the distillery in 1794, when there was barely a town on the bay, and Oban grew up around it: the producer calls it the town that whisky built. The brothers' family ran it until 1866, when it was sold, and in 1883 it changed hands again and was rebuilt. Hemmed in by the streets that grew around it, it has stayed small, with one wash still and one spirit still of the old lantern shape. Outside among the rooftops, wooden worm tubs condense the spirit slowly in the salt air, where most distilleries use modern condensers. The 14 Year Old is the house's standing bottling and became its West Highland entry in the Classic Malts, a set of single malts chosen to show the regions of Scotland. For a bartender it is the coastal Highland malt a guest asks for by name: orange zest, fruit bread, clove and a little salt, from a distillery in the middle of a working port.

records.table: The Dalmore 12 Year Old is the sherried Highland malt from Alness on the Cromarty Firth, the bottle with the twelve-pointed stag. It starts in bourbon casks and part of it moves to Oloroso sherry casks: Seville orange, chocolate and dried fruit, a natural Rob Roy.
records.story: Alexander Matheson (1805 to 1886), a China merchant and later a member of Parliament, founded the distillery at Alness in 1839, on the site of a mill and farm on the Cromarty Firth. In 1867 the Mackenzie family took over the running of it, and in 1891 they bought it outright from his son. They brought their clan's emblem with them, the twelve-pointed royal stag that stands on every bottle. As the brand tells it, the stag recalls 1263, when a Mackenzie chief is said to have saved the King of Scots from a charging stag; the story is legend. The family's firm kept the distillery until 1960, when it merged with the blenders Whyte & Mackay, one of its customers. The stills are part of the house style: flat-topped wash stills, and spirit stills with water jackets round their necks to raise reflux. The 12 Year Old gives that spirit bourbon casks and then Oloroso. For a bartender it is the plain Highland example of what sherry does to a malt: orange peel, dried fruit and chocolate.

records.table: Dalwhinnie 15 Year Old is the gentle Highland malt from a distillery more than a thousand feet up in the Central Highlands. Expect heather honey, vanilla and citrus with only a wisp of peat at the end; pour it neat or with a little water.
records.story: The distillery was built in 1897 under the name Strathspey and ran its first spirit in February 1898. Its first owners soon failed, and in 1898 it was sold and renamed Dalwhinnie, from the Gaelic for a meeting place. In 1905 it was sold to Cook & Bernheimer, distillers of New York and Baltimore, so a Highland distillery passed into American hands. When Prohibition came to the United States in 1919 they sold it to Macdonald Greenlees, blenders of Leith, and in 1926 that firm was taken into the Distillers Company. The village stands high in the Central Highlands, more than a thousand feet above the sea, and the distillery's worm tubs, coils of pipe in tubs of cold water outside the still house, were taken out in a modernisation and later put back. The 15 Year Old is the bottling a guest will meet: honey, heather and vanilla, with only a hint of peat. For a bartender it is the malt to reach for when a guest new to Scotch asks for something gentle, and the proof that Highland need not mean smoke or sherry.

records.table: Clynelish 14 Year Old is the Highland malt from Brora on the Sutherland coast, known for a waxy texture as much as for its taste. Expect candle wax, dried flowers and a little salt over a creamy body; a few drops of water bring the wax up.
records.story: The Sutherland estate built the original Clynelish at Brora in 1819, in the years of the Sutherland Clearances, to give its smaller tenants a lawful market for their grain, with coal from the estate's own pit at Brora to fire the stills. Through the nineteenth and twentieth centuries its spirit went mainly into blends. In 1967 and 1968 a new Clynelish distillery was built on the next plot, and the name moved to it. The old still house worked on for a time under the name Brora, closed in 1983, and was brought back to work in 2021, so two distilleries now stand side by side. The new Clynelish kept the old house's waxy spirit, a character writers trace to the oily deposits in its feints receiver. Its spirit has long gone into Johnnie Walker, and the producer counts Clynelish among the Four Corners distilleries of Johnnie Walker. The 14 Year Old is the bottling a guest meets. For a bartender it is the malt that teaches texture as a distillery character: wax, flowers and salt from a still house on the northern coast.
